title: Reason Through SAT Survey Questions
description: Evaluate survey samples, limit conclusions to the correct population, and interpret margin of error as a plausible range.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep your first idea, even if you are unsure. You can continue without submitting an answer.

  1. Exactly \(58\%\) of all adults living in the city support the extension.
  2. It is plausible that between \(54\%\) and \(62\%\) of adults on the city's voter rolls support the extension.
  3. The true level of support among the \(400\) respondents is between \(54\%\) and \(62\%\).
  4. Support cannot be estimated, because just \(400\) of the city's adults were surveyed.

shared_prompt.title: Opening question
shared_prompt.html: A parks department randomly selects \(400\) adults from the city's voter rolls and asks whether they support extending trail hours at the city's three largest parks. \(58\%\) answer yes, with a margin of error of \(4\) percentage points. Which statement is best supported by these results?

blocks.html:
Decide who the survey can describe

The parks question combines two decisions: whose opinion was sampled, and how certain its estimate is. We’ll learn to separate those decisions.

Start with a school survey so you can compare ways to choose respondents before interpreting any percentages.

shared_prompt.title: School start-time survey
shared_prompt.html: A principal wants to estimate what all students at a high school think about a later start time.

blocks.html:
Choose a sample for the school

To estimate all students’ opinions, compare asking library visitors, inviting social-media volunteers, sampling randomly from the complete enrollment list, or asking student council members. Which plan gives the whole school a fair chance to be represented?

content.prompt: Which plan is best designed to estimate the opinion of all students at the school?
choices: Ask the first 100 students who enter the library.
Post an optional poll on the school's social media account and count the replies.
Randomly select students from the complete school enrollment list.
Ask every member of the student council.
content.hint: Look for a method that starts with the entire group of students and does not depend on volunteering or visiting one location.
content.explanation: A random selection from the complete enrollment list gives students across the school a chance to be included and avoids relying on one convenient or self-selected group.

blocks.html:
Name the whole group and the observed part

The target population is the group you want to describe. The sample is the part surveyed. A sample statistic, such as the percent answering yes, is known for that sample; it estimates the population’s corresponding value.

content.prompt: A random sample of 250 students is surveyed, and 64% of that sample supports a new schedule. Which statement is known from the survey data?
choices: Exactly 64% of the sampled students support the schedule.
Exactly 64% of the school's entire student body supports the schedule.
Any other group of 250 students at the school would also produce 64%.
The unsurveyed students must have the same opinions as the sample.
content.hint: Separate what was directly measured in the sample from what must be estimated about the population.
content.explanation: The 64% is an exact description of the surveyed sample. It can estimate the population only with appropriate sampling and uncertainty.

blocks.html:
Use a selection method that represents the group

An unbiased method does not systematically favor a relevant kind of member. Random selection from a list covering the target population helps achieve this.

A random sample can differ from the population by chance. That uncertainty is different from a selection method that favors one group.

Notice who gets into the sample

  • Convenience sampling: whoever is easiest to reach.
  • Voluntary response: people choose themselves.
  • Undercoverage: part of the target group cannot be selected.

A large sample does not repair these selection problems.

content.prompt: A city wants to estimate the opinions of all adult residents. Which method is most clearly biased?
choices: Randomly select adults from a complete city resident list and survey each selected adult.
Randomly select adults from each neighborhood in proportion to neighborhood size.
Randomly select addresses across the city and select one adult from each chosen household.
Invite visitors to the city website to choose whether to complete the survey.
content.hint: Which method allows people with strong opinions or frequent website use to select themselves?
content.explanation: Website visitors who volunteer may differ systematically from the full adult population, creating voluntary-response bias.

blocks.html:
Check what happens after selection too

Nonresponse bias can occur when respondents differ meaningfully from selected people who do not answer. Leading wording can also push answers: “the sensible plan” suggests a preference that a neutral question would not.

content.prompt: A company randomly selects customers for a satisfaction survey, but dissatisfied customers are much more likely to respond than satisfied customers. What is the main concern?
choices: The target population of customers is too large for any survey to estimate.
Nonresponse may bias the results because respondents differ from nonrespondents.
The random selection itself failed, so none of the collected responses can be trusted.
The company must survey each of its customers before making any estimate.
content.hint: The original selection was random, but compare the people who answered with those who did not.
content.explanation: If response behavior is related to satisfaction, the respondents can overrepresent one opinion even though the initial sample was random.

blocks.html:
Keep every restriction on the sampled group

A random sample of district eleventh graders can support estimates about district eleventh graders. It cannot automatically describe all district students or all statewide eleventh graders.

The selection process determines how far you can generalize.

content.prompt: A district randomly selects 300 students from a complete list of all eleventh-grade students in the district. What is the largest population to which the results can be generalized?
choices: All high school students across the entire state
All students in the district
All eleventh-grade students in the district
Only the 300 students who responded
content.hint: Preserve both restrictions in the selection group: grade level and district.
content.explanation: The random selection represents all eleventh-grade students in that district, but it does not represent other grades or other districts.

content.prompt: A random sample of registered voters in County M finds that 48% support a proposal. Which statement is best supported?
choices: The data suggest that about 48% of registered voters in County M support the proposal.
Exactly 48% of County M's full resident population supports the proposal.
About 48% of registered voters throughout the country support the proposal.
Each future sample drawn from County M's voters will again contain exactly 48% support.
content.hint: Keep the population as registered voters in County M and avoid claiming an exact population value.
content.explanation: The conclusion keeps the correct target population and treats the sample result as an estimate rather than an exact fact.

content.prompt: A well-designed random sample finds that 84% of sampled households use a recycling service. Which conclusion is not supported?
choices: The sample statistic is 84%.
The population proportion is likely to be somewhere near 84%.
The true population proportion may differ from 84%.
Exactly 84% of all households use the recycling service.
content.hint: Which choice incorrectly turns a sample estimate into an exact population fact?
content.explanation: The sample percentage is known, but the population percentage is estimated and may differ because of sampling variation.

blocks.html:
Include sampling uncertainty

The margin of error gives a reported amount of sampling uncertainty around an estimate. Move that many percentage points below and above the sample percent.

Subtract and add

For 57% with margin of error 3 percentage points, calculate 57-3=54 and 57+3=60. The plausible population range is 54% to 60%.

content.prompt: A random-sample survey reports 46% support with a margin of error of 5 percentage points. What is the plausible range for the population proportion?
content.hint: Subtract 5 points from 46 for the lower end, then add 5 points to 46 for the upper end.
content.explanation: 46 − 5 = 41 and 46 + 5 = 51, so the plausible population range is 41% to 51%.

blocks.html:
An estimate is not exact or guaranteed

A reported interval gives plausible population values under the survey’s method. The true value can still lie outside it. Use “estimated” or “plausible” rather than claiming certainty.

Margin of error does not remove selection bias or leading wording.

content.prompt: A survey reports 62% with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which interpretation is most accurate?
choices: The survey shows that exactly 62% of the population holds the measured opinion.
The true population value must fall somewhere between 58% and 66%.
Values from 58% to 66% are plausible, but the true population value could be outside that range.
Any population value from 4% to 62% is equally likely to be correct.
content.hint: Build the interval, then choose wording that treats it as likely rather than guaranteed.
content.explanation: The margin of error creates a plausible interval of 58% to 66%, but a statistical interval is not an absolute guarantee.

blocks.html:
A larger random sample improves precision

With the survey design and other conditions unchanged, increasing sample size reduces margin of error. It gives a more precise estimate; it does not make the estimate certain.

content.prompt: Researchers will repeat the same random-sample survey. Which change will reduce the margin of error?
choices: Increase the sample from 400 people to 1,600 people.
Survey the same 400 people with a more strongly worded question.
Replace the random sample with 400 volunteers.
Apply the results to a larger target population.
content.hint: Keep the survey design the same and change only how many randomly selected people are sampled.
content.explanation: Increasing the random sample size reduces sampling variability and therefore reduces the margin of error.

blocks.html:
Selection and size solve different problems

Representative selection protects against systematic bias. A larger sample reduces random sampling uncertainty. More volunteers can still give a biased result, even in a very large poll.

content.prompt: An online poll collects 10,000 voluntary responses. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The very large sample guarantees that the poll accurately represents the target population.
The poll has no uncertainty because more than 1,000 people responded.
A margin of error would automatically correct any voluntary-response bias.
The large sample does not remove bias caused by allowing respondents to select themselves.
content.hint: Ask whether adding more volunteers changes how those people entered the sample.
content.explanation: Sample size can improve precision, but it cannot fix a selection method that systematically overrepresents volunteers.

shared_prompt.title: District tutoring-period survey
shared_prompt.html: A school district randomly selects 400 eleventh-grade students from its complete list of eleventh graders. Of the sampled students, 54% support a new tutoring period. The margin of error is 3 percentage points.

blocks.html:
Put scope and uncertainty together

The district sampled eleventh graders randomly and found 54% support, with margin of error 3 percentage points. The plausible range is 51% to 57%, for district eleventh graders. It does not guarantee the true value or describe a broader group.

content.prompt: Which conclusion best matches the district survey?
choices: Exactly 54% of the district's entire student body supports the tutoring period.
It is plausible that 51% to 57% of the district's eleventh-grade students support the tutoring period.
At least 51% of high school students statewide support the tutoring period.
The true support among district eleventh graders cannot be outside 51% to 57%.
content.hint: Keep the population as district eleventh graders, use the 51% to 57% range, and avoid a guarantee.
content.explanation: This choice preserves the sampled population, uses the margin-of-error interval, and describes the range as plausible.

blocks.html:
Name, Check, Limit, Range

  1. Name the population and sample.
  2. Check how respondents were selected.
  3. Limit the conclusion to the represented population and measured feature.
  4. If given a margin of error, subtract and add it to form a plausible range.

Return to the parks survey

Try the opening question again. Check who the sample represents and what the reported uncertainty allows you to say.

content.prompt: Return to the opening question. What answer do you get now?
choices: Exactly \(58\%\) of all adults living in the city support the extension.
It is plausible that between \(54\%\) and \(62\%\) of adults on the city's voter rolls support the extension.
The true level of support among the \(400\) respondents is between \(54\%\) and \(62\%\).
Support cannot be estimated, because just \(400\) of the city's adults were surveyed.
content.hint: Keep the conclusion about the adults on the voter rolls, the group sampled. Add and subtract 4 percentage points from 58 and interpret that interval as plausible.
content.explanation: \(58-4=54\) and \(58+4=62\), and the claim stays with adults on the voter rolls — the sampled population. Among the \(400\) respondents support is exactly \(58\%\), so no interval applies to them, and a random sample of \(400\) does permit an estimate.
content.solution: \(58-4=54\) and \(58+4=62\), and the claim stays with adults on the voter rolls — the sampled population. Among the \(400\) respondents support is exactly \(58\%\), so no interval applies to them, and a random sample of \(400\) does permit an estimate.

content.prompt: What do you check before making a population claim from a survey with a margin of error?
choices: Identify the population, audit selection for bias, extend the claim to any similar population, and use plus/minus margin of error as a guaranteed range.
Identify the population, audit selection for bias, limit the claim to that population, and use plus/minus margin of error as a plausible—not guaranteed—range.
Audit selection for bias only when the sample is small, identify the population afterward, and subtract the margin of error from the reported result.
Identify the population, trust any large sample regardless of selection, limit the claim to that population, and drop the plus/minus range once the sample is big enough.
content.explanation: You have it. A trustworthy inference begins with representative random selection, stays inside the represented population, and treats the margin-of-error interval as plausible rather than certain.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: A university randomly samples 250 students from a complete list of its first-year students. What is the largest population to which the results can be generalized?
choices: All university students throughout the country
All students at that university
All first-year students at that university
Only the 250 sampled first-year students
content.explanation: The random sample represents all first-year students at that university, not other class years or other universities.

content.prompt: A town randomly samples households from a complete address list, and 38% of the sampled households compost food waste. Which statement is best supported?
choices: The data suggest that about 38% of households in the town compost food waste.
Exactly 38% of households in the town compost food waste.
About 38% of households in the state compost food waste.
Composting food waste causes households to participate more readily in town surveys.
content.explanation: The conclusion uses cautious language and stays within the town households represented by the random sample.

content.prompt: A valid random-sample survey reports 71% with a margin of error of 6 percentage points. Which population range is plausible?
content.explanation: 71 − 6 = 65 and 71 + 6 = 77, so 65% to 77% is the plausible range.

content.html:
Check the Sample, Limit the Claim

Keep the represented population and the uncertainty in your answer.
